cluster: Understand the relationship between zeros and factors of polynomials
skillName: Understand the relationship between zeros and factors of polynomials
intro: End-of-cluster mastery check on the relationship between zeros and factors of polynomials. Items 1 to 6 cover the Remainder and Factor Theorems (A2.A-APR.B.2); items 7 to 12 cover zeros, multiplicity, and polynomial graphs (A2.A-APR.B.3).

items.prompt:
Find the remainder when $p(x)=x^3-4x^2+2x-5$ is divided by $x-3$.
A) $-8$
B) $-2$
C) $8$
D) $0$

steps: By the Remainder Theorem, the remainder of $p(x)\div(x-a)$ equals $p(a)$. Here the divisor is $x-3$, so $a=3$.
The remainder is $-8$, choice A.
B ($-2$) drops the $-5$ constant. C ($8$) is just $3^3$ with the wrong sign handling. D ($0$) would mean $x-3$ is a factor, but $p(3)\ne 0$.

items.prompt:
Which statement correctly applies the Factor Theorem to $p(x)=x^3-x^2-4x+4$ given that $p(2)=0$?
A) $(x-2)$ is a factor of $p(x)$
B) $(x+2)$ is a factor of $p(x)$
C) $(x-2)$ is not a factor of $p(x)$
D) $2$ is the remainder when $p(x)$ is divided by $x-2$

steps: The Factor Theorem says $(x-a)$ is a factor of $p(x)$ if and only if $p(a)=0$.
We are told $p(2)=0$, so taking $a=2$ gives that $(x-2)$ is a factor. This is choice A.
B uses the wrong sign: $p(2)=0$ corresponds to $(x-2)$, not $(x+2)$.
C reverses the theorem, denying a factor when $p(a)=0$. D is wrong because $p(2)=0$ means the remainder is $0$, not $2$.

items.prompt:
Find the remainder when $p(x)=2x^3+5x^2-3$ is divided by $x+2$.
A) $1$
B) $33$
C) $-3$
D) $5$

steps: The divisor is $x+2=x-(-2)$, so $a=-2$.
Note the missing $x$ term: $p(x)=2x^3+5x^2+0x-3$.
The remainder is $1$, choice A. B ($33$) comes from using $a=2$ instead of $-2$. C ($-3$) ignores the cubic and quadratic terms. D ($5$) misreads a coefficient as the remainder.

items.prompt:
Using synthetic division, what is the remainder when $p(x)=x^3-2x^2-5x+6$ is divided by $x-3$?
A) $0$
B) $-2$
C) $1$
D) $6$

steps: Set up synthetic division with $a=3$ and coefficients $1,\ -2,\ -5,\ 6$.
Bring down $1$. Multiply $1\cdot 3=3$, add to $-2$ to get $1$. Multiply $1\cdot 3=3$, add to $-5$ to get $-2$. Multiply $-2\cdot 3=-6$, add to $6$ to get $0$.
The last entry, $0$, is the remainder, so the remainder is $0$ (and $x-3$ is a factor). This is choice A.
B ($-2$) and C ($1$) are middle entries of the synthetic row (quotient coefficients), not the remainder. D ($6$) is the original constant term.

items.prompt:
Find the value of $k$ so that $x-2$ is a factor of $p(x)=x^3+kx-6$.
A) $k=-1$
B) $k=1$
C) $k=-7$
D) $k=3$

steps: For $(x-2)$ to be a factor, the Factor Theorem requires $p(2)=0$.
Set $2+2k=0$, so $2k=-2$ and $k=-1$. This is choice A.
B ($k=1$) comes from a sign slip on the constant. C ($k=-7$) sets $p(2)=2$ instead of $0$ in part. D ($k=3$) ignores the $-6$ term when solving.

items.prompt:
Is $2x-1$ a factor of $p(x)=2x^3+x^2-1$?
A) No, because $p\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)=-\tfrac{1}{2}\ne 0$
B) Yes, because $p\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)=0$
C) No, because $p(2)=19\ne 0$
D) Yes, because $p\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\right)=0$

steps: Set $2x-1=0$ to find the value to test: $x=\tfrac{1}{2}$.
Evaluate $p\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)=2\cdot\tfrac{1}{8}+\tfrac{1}{4}-1=\tfrac{1}{4}+\tfrac{1}{4}-1=-\tfrac{1}{2}$.
Since $p\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)=-\tfrac{1}{2}\ne 0$, $2x-1$ is not a factor. This is choice A.

C tests at $x=2$, the wrong value for a divisor with leading coefficient $2$. B and D claim a zero remainder, but the correct value is $-\tfrac{1}{2}$, and D also uses the wrong sign $x=-\tfrac{1}{2}$.
Set each factor equal to $0$ (Zero Product Property).
$x-2=0\Rightarrow x=2$; $x+5=0\Rightarrow x=-5$; $x-1=0\Rightarrow x=1$.
The zeros are $x=2,\ x=-5,\ x=1$, choice A.
B negates every zero (wrong sign on all factors). C mishandles the sign on $x+5$. D negates all three constants.
The $y$-intercept is $f(0)$.
So the $y$-intercept is $(0,-6)$, choice A.
B drops the negative sign. C drops the leading factor of $2$. D mistakes the leading coefficient $2$ for the intercept.

items.prompt:
For $f(x)=(x+1)^2(x-3)$, what is the behavior of the graph at each zero?
A) Tangent at $x=-1$ (multiplicity $2$); crosses at $x=3$ (multiplicity $1$)
B) Crosses at $x=-1$ (multiplicity $2$); tangent at $x=3$ (multiplicity $1$)
C) Tangent at $x=1$ and crosses at $x=-3$
D) Crosses at both $x=-1$ and $x=3$

steps: Zeros come from each factor: $x=-1$ (from $(x+1)^2$) and $x=3$ (from $(x-3)$).
Even multiplicity ($2$) means the graph is tangent to the axis (touches and turns); odd multiplicity ($1$) means it crosses.
So the graph is tangent at $x=-1$ and crosses at $x=3$. This is choice A.
B reverses the touch-vs-cross rule. C reads the zeros with the wrong signs. D ignores multiplicity entirely.

items.prompt:
Find all real zeros of $f(x)=x^3-4x$.
A) $x=0,\ x=2,\ x=-2$
B) $x=2,\ x=-2$
C) $x=0,\ x=4$
D) $x=0,\ x=2$

steps: Factor out the GCF: $f(x)=x(x^2-4)$.
Recognize the difference of squares: $x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)$, so $f(x)=x(x-2)(x+2)$.
Set each factor to $0$: $x=0,\ x=2,\ x=-2$. This is choice A.
B drops the $x=0$ zero (forgets the GCF factor). D misses $x=-2$ (incomplete difference of squares). C fails to factor $x^2-4$ at all.
Treat the expression as a quadratic in $x^2$: $x^4-5x^2+4=(x^2-1)(x^2-4)$.
Factor each difference of squares: $(x^2-1)=(x-1)(x+1)$ and $(x^2-4)=(x-2)(x+2)$.
So $f(x)=(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)(x+2)$, giving zeros $x=1,\ x=-1,\ x=2,\ x=-2$. This is choice A.
B stops at $x^2=1$ and $x^2=4$ without taking both roots. C and D each keep only one of the two difference-of-squares factors.

items.prompt:
Which factored polynomial has zeros only at $x=-3$ and $x=1$, is tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=1$, and falls on both ends (as $x\to\pm\infty$, $f(x)\to-\infty$)?
A) $f(x)=-(x+3)(x-1)^2$
B) $f(x)=(x+3)(x-1)^2$
C) $f(x)=-(x-3)(x+1)^2$
D) $f(x)=-(x+3)^2(x-1)$

steps: Zeros at $x=-3$ and $x=1$ require factors $(x+3)$ and $(x-1)$.
Tangent at $x=1$ means that zero has even multiplicity, so the factor is $(x-1)^2$; the zero at $x=-3$ is a simple crossing, factor $(x+3)$.
The degree is $3$ (odd). For both ends to fall, the leading coefficient must be negative, so a front minus sign is needed: $f(x)=-(x+3)(x-1)^2$. This is choice A.
B has a positive leading coefficient, so its ends do not both fall. C puts the tangency at the wrong zero ($x=-1$, $x=3$). D makes $x=-3$ the tangent (squared) zero instead of $x=1$.
